segments: The ninth period.
The Christian Greek Emperors.
And they made a journey of two months in the winter season,
because of the abundance of water,
that is to say, from the passes of Mount Amanus {Caucasus?}.
And they arrived as far as the Tanais (Don),
the river Don {editor query: Duna?},
that which issues from Lake Maeotis,
and empties into the Pontic Sea.
And when they reached the territory of the Romans,
one of them whose name was Bulgaris took ten thousand [men],
and crossed the Tanais,
and pitched his camp {tent?} between the two rivers, the Tanais and the Dunbis (Danube and Dnieper?),
which also empties into the Pontic Sea.
And he sent to Maurice [asking] that he would give him land to dwell in,
and that he would become an ally to the Romans.
And he gave him Upper and Lower Moesia,
and they settled there,
and became a guard for the Romans.
And although they were Scythians,
the Romans called them Bulgarians.
These two other brothers, however, came to the land of the Alans, that is Barsalia, that is, to the cities of Caspia {or: Cappadocia? or perhaps Qipchaq?},
which the Bulgarians and Pangurians and Pazgorians {and Hungarians?} call the Gate of the Turks, who were formerly Christians,
and now are called Khazars after the name of that elder brother.
And in the sixth year of Maurice,
Priscus, the general of the Romans, marched down against Persia with a large army,
and there the Romans mutinied against him and did not accept him.
Then the Emperor reversed [matters] and appointed as their general Philippicus, his brother-in-law, his sister's husband.
And when he went down,
he showed many triumphs.
The Romans, however, because they had become accustomed to the rebellion that had been against Priscus,
began to provoke this one too.
And they plotted to depose the Emperor also,
and to set up another.
And when they returned from Persia to Antioch and wintered there,
a great earthquake occurred,
and the greater part of the city fell in the tremor,
and the army was scattered into the environs of the city.
And the horsemen who had resisted the Emperor repented,
and they turned back and were reconciled with Philippicus.
And when they were reconciled,
they heard that the Persians of Nisibis had seduced the guards of Mayperqat with gifts,
and they had surrendered the city to them,
and many Romans had perished in it.
Philippicus and the Romans quickly set out from Antioch for Mayperqat,
and he took it by battle,
